questions.q: A stack is a collection of items in which insertion and removal can take place only at one end. What ordering discipline does this produce?
questions.e: A stack allows insertion and removal only at the top, so the last item pushed is the first popped. This makes it a LIFO (last in, first out) structure.

questions.q: The single end of a stack at which all insertions and deletions occur is called what?
questions.e: In a stack, both insertion (push) and removal (pop) happen only at one end, called the top of the stack.

questions.q: Which operation adds a new item to a stack, and which removes one?
o: Push adds to the top; Pop removes from the top
questions.e: Push adds a new item onto the top of the stack, and Pop removes the item from the top of the stack.

questions.q: Attempting to push an item onto a stack that is already full produces which condition?
questions.e: Pushing onto a full stack causes stack overflow. Popping from an empty stack causes stack underflow.

questions.q: Attempting to pop an item from an empty stack produces which condition?
questions.e: Removing an item from an empty stack causes stack underflow, whereas adding to a full stack causes stack overflow.

questions.q: In a typical array-based stack whose default constructor sets top to -1, which test correctly reports that the stack is empty?
questions.e: The default constructor initialises top to -1 for an empty stack, so IsEmpty returns true exactly when top == -1. IsFull returns true when top == MAX_ITEMS - 1.

questions.q: In an array-based stack that stores elements in items[0..MAX_ITEMS-1], which condition indicates the stack is full?
questions.e: Since valid indices run from 0 to MAX_ITEMS-1, the stack is full when top has reached MAX_ITEMS - 1, the last usable slot.

questions.q: When a function is called, what structure is used to store its return address, parameters, local variables and return value?
o: An activation record (stack frame) on the run-time stack
questions.e: Each function call places an activation record (stack frame) on the run-time stack; it stores the return address, the parameters, the local variables, and the function's return value if non-void.

questions.q: When is the activation record for a function call removed from the run-time stack?
o: When the final closing brace or a return statement in the function is reached
When a new variable is declared
questions.e: The activation record is popped off the run-time stack when the final closing brace of the function is reached, or when a return statement is executed; the return value, if any, is then passed back to the calling block.

questions.q: Which of these is given as a fundamental application of stacks?
o: Scheduling CPU tasks in first-come order
Serving customers at a supermarket checkout
questions.e: Applications of stacks include implementing function calls and recursion, checking whether symbols balance in an expression, and reversing a sequence or string. First-come service and prioritised items are queue applications.

questions.q: In the parenthesis-count method for checking balanced symbols, what two conditions must hold for an expression to be valid?
o: The count must be positive at the end and negative at some point
The count must be 0 at the end and non-negative at every point
The count must equal the number of operators
The count must be odd at the end
questions.e: Each left parenthesis adds one to the count and each right subtracts one. A valid expression requires the parenthesis count to be 0 at the end and non-negative at every point along the way.

questions.q: When using a stack to check balanced brackets, what should happen when a closing symbol such as ) ] or } is read?
o: If the stack is empty report an error; otherwise pop and check it matches the corresponding opening symbol
questions.e: On reading a closing symbol, if the stack is empty an error is reported; otherwise the stack is popped, and if the popped symbol is not the corresponding opening symbol an error is reported. Opening symbols are pushed.

questions.q: In the notation for arithmetic expressions, where is the operator placed in infix, postfix and prefix forms respectively for A + B?
o: A+B is postfix; AB+ is prefix; +AB is infix
A+B is infix; AB+ is postfix; +AB is prefix
A+B is prefix; AB+ is infix; +AB is postfix
questions.e: For A + B: infix places the operator between operands (A + B), postfix places it after (AB+), and prefix places it before (+AB).

questions.q: What is a key advantage of postfix notation for representing arithmetic expressions?
o: It always needs parentheses to show grouping
There is never any need to use parentheses
It requires two stacks to evaluate
questions.e: Postfix is regarded as the most efficient way to represent arithmetic expressions because there is never any need to use parentheses to indicate order of operations.

questions.q: What is the postfix form of the infix expression (A + B) * (C - D)?
questions.e: Converting (A + B) * (C - D) to postfix gives AB+CD-*; the prefix form is *+AB-CD.

questions.q: What is the prefix form of the infix expression (A + B) * (C - D)?
questions.e: The prefix form of (A + B) * (C - D) is *+AB-CD, while its postfix form is AB+CD-*.

questions.q: Evaluating the postfix expression 6 2 3 + - using a stack gives what result?
questions.e: Push 6, 2, 3. The + pops 2 and 3 giving 5, leaving 6 and 5. The - computes 6 - 5 = 1, so the result is 1.

questions.q: In the postfix evaluation algorithm, what is done when the scanned symbol is an operator?
o: Push the operator onto the stack
Pop the top two operands, apply the operator, and push the result
Pop one operand and negate it
questions.e: When an operand is read it is pushed. When an operator is read, the top two operands are popped, the operation is performed on them, and the result is pushed back onto the stack.

questions.q: In the infix-to-postfix conversion algorithm, what is done when a right parenthesis ')' is read from the input?
o: Pop and output operators until a '(' is found on the stack, then discard the '(' without output
Clear the entire stack and output it
questions.e: On reading ')', the algorithm pops and outputs all operators until a '(' appears on the stack, then pops that '(' without outputting it. A '(' in the input is simply pushed.

questions.q: A recursive definition must include which essential component to ensure the recursion eventually stops?
questions.e: A recursive definition has two components: a base case (which stops the recursion) and a recursive case (which defines the object in terms of a simpler case of itself).

questions.q: Using the recursive definition where n! = 1 if n = 0 and n! = n*(n-1)! if n > 0, what is the base case?
questions.e: The recursive relationship is n! = n*(n-1)! for n > 0, and the base case is 0! = 1 (with 1! also equal to 1), which stops the recursion.

questions.q: Using the recursive definition x^0 = 1 and x^n = x * x^(n-1), how is the power function's base case defined?
questions.e: For the power function, the base case is x^0 = 1, and the general (recursive) case is x^n = x * x^(n-1) for n > 0.

questions.q: Using the recursive definition of multiplication where a*b = a if b = 1 and a*b = a*(b-1) + a if b > 1, what is the value of 6*3?
questions.e: 6*3 = 6*2 + 6 = (6*1 + 6) + 6 = 6 + 6 + 6 = 18, applying the recursive definition until the base case b = 1.

questions.q: For the Fibonacci sequence defined by fib(n) = 1 if n = 1 or n = 2, and fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) if n > 2, what is fib(6)?
questions.e: The sequence is 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ..., so fib(6) = fib(5) + fib(4) = 5 + 3 = 8.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of recursion compared with an iterative solution?
o: It is harder to prove correct
It may run slower and use more space
It is less natural to express
questions.e: Recursion's advantages include being more natural, easier to prove correct, easier to analyse and more flexible; its disadvantages are that it may run slower and may use more space.

questions.q: A queue adds new elements at one end and removes elements from the other. What ordering discipline does this give?
questions.e: In a queue, elements are added at the rear and removed from the front, so the first element inserted is the first removed. This is a FIFO (first in, first out) structure.

questions.q: In a queue, from which end are elements removed and at which end are they added?
o: Removed from the rear, added at the front
Removed from the front, added at the rear
Both operations occur at the top
Both operations occur at the front
questions.e: New elements are added at the rear of the queue, and elements are removed from the front, which produces the FIFO ordering.

questions.q: Which everyday situation best models a queue data structure?
o: A stack of plates where you take the top one
Customers waiting in first-come-first-served order at a checkout
questions.e: Queues model first-come-first-served systems such as supermarket checkouts, banks, airports and petrol stations, where clients wait in arrival order for service.

questions.q: Which pair of names is used for the operations that add and remove items in a queue ADT?
o: Insert (add at rear) and Remove (take from front)
Enqueue and Dequeue from the same end
questions.e: The queue ADT defines Insert, which adds a new item at the rear, and Remove, which takes the item from the front and returns it.

questions.q: Why is a plain linear-array implementation of a queue considered expensive?
o: It cannot store more than one element
When an item is removed from the front, all remaining elements must be shifted down by one
It requires the data to be sorted first
questions.e: In a linear array all removals come from element 0, so after each removal every remaining element must be shifted down by one position, which is expensive.

questions.q: In a circular array queue, how is the 'wrap-around' of the rear pointer accomplished?
questions.e: Wrap-around is achieved with the modulo operator: rear = (rear + 1) % maxQue (and similarly for front), so the index returns to the start of the array after reaching the end.

questions.q: In a circular queue that uses front and rear indices, which condition signals that the queue is full (overflow)?
questions.e: The circular queue is full when the rear is one spot 'behind' the front, i.e. front == (rear + 1) % maxQue.

questions.q: In the queue convention where an empty queue is marked by front and rear equal to -1, what must be done after deleting the last remaining element?
o: Set both front and rear to -1
questions.e: When the last element is deleted, both front and rear are reset to -1 to mark the queue empty. When the first element is inserted into an empty queue, both are set to 0.

questions.q: In the count-based circular queue template, the IsFull operation returns true under which condition?
questions.e: The count-based implementation tracks the number of items in 'count'; IsFull returns (count == maxQue) and IsEmpty returns (count == 0).

questions.q: What distinguishes a priority queue from an ordinary FIFO queue?
o: Items can only be added, never removed
Items are ranked by priority, and priority (not arrival order) determines which item is removed
It can hold only one item at a time
It removes items in reverse insertion order
questions.e: A priority queue holds prioritised items; the priority of elements determines the result of operations, so a higher-priority item is served before a lower-priority one even if it arrived later.

questions.q: In an ascending priority queue, which item can be removed?
questions.e: An ascending priority queue allows removal of only the smallest item, whereas a descending priority queue allows removal of only the largest item.

questions.q: A descending priority queue allows deletion of which item?
questions.e: A descending priority queue permits deletion of only the largest item; an ascending priority queue permits removal of only the smallest.

questions.q: One way to implement a priority queue is to insert items in sorted order and always remove the head. What is the trade-off of the alternative (insert unordered, search on remove)?
o: Both insertion and removal become instant
Either insertion is slow and removal quick, or insertion is quick and removal slow
It requires the items to have no priority
questions.e: Whichever approach is used, the total time is comparable: either adding data takes time and removal is quick (sorted insert), or adding is quick and removal takes time (unordered insert with search).

questions.q: How is a double-ended queue (deque) defined?
o: A queue where elements can be added or removed at either end but not in the middle
A queue with two separate fronts
A queue that stores each element twice
A queue that can only grow, never shrink
questions.e: A deque (double-ended queue) is a queue in which elements can be added or removed at either end, but not in the middle.

questions.q: What is the difference between an input-restricted deque and an output-restricted deque?
o: Input-restricted allows deletions from one end only; output-restricted allows insertions from one end only
Input-restricted allows insertions from one end only; output-restricted allows deletions from one end only
Both restrict insertions to one end
questions.e: An input-restricted deque allows insertions from one end only, while an output-restricted deque allows deletions from one end only; both still permit the other operation at either end.

questions.q: In the given deque implementation, what pointers are maintained and on what kind of array?
o: A single TOP pointer on a linear array
LEFT and RIGHT pointers on a circular array
FRONT and REAR pointers on a linked stack
A HEAD pointer on a doubly linked list
questions.e: A deque is maintained using a circular array with two pointers, LEFT and RIGHT, which point to the two ends of the deque.

questions.q: In operating systems, queues are commonly used for which purpose?
o: Regulating tasks such as CPU scheduling and managing shared resources like the printer
questions.e: Operating systems use queues of task records to regulate work; jobs wait in queues for service by shared resources such as the printer, the CPU and storage devices (CPU scheduling, resource management).

questions.q: In queueing/simulation studies, which of the following is a typical performance measure of interest?
o: The average waiting time, queue length, or throughput (clients served per hour)
questions.e: When queues are used to model systems where clients arrive and receive service, measures of interest include the average waiting time, the length of the queue, and the throughput (number of clients served per hour).

questions.q: Which of the following is a limitation of arrays that linked lists overcome?
o: An array's size is fixed at construction time and ordered insertion requires shifting many elements
questions.e: Arrays are simple and fast (indexed) but their size is fixed at construction (static) with contiguous memory, and ordered insertion is time-consuming because many elements must be shifted. Linked lists are dynamic and grow as needed.

questions.q: A linked list is best described as which of the following?
o: A block of contiguous memory of fixed size
A collection or chain of nodes where each node references the next and the last references null
questions.e: A linked list is a chain of nodes in which each node references the next node in the chain and the last node references null. Each node holds the data plus a pointer to the next node.

questions.q: In a singly linked list, what does each node contain?
o: The data (info) and a pointer to the next node
A key and an array index
questions.e: Each node of a singly linked list contains the data (the info portion) and a pointer (next) to the following node in the chain.

questions.q: In a linked list, what are the head node and the tail node?
o: The head is the middle node; the tail is the root
The head is the first node; the tail is the last node
The head is the last node; the tail is the first node
Both refer to the same node
questions.e: The head node is the first node of the list, and the tail node is the last node; the tail's next pointer references null.

questions.q: Using the algorithmic notation where info(p) and next(p) refer to a node's data and next pointer, which sequence correctly inserts a new node x at the front of a list called 'list'?
questions.e: To insert at the front: get a new node p, store x in info(p), set next(p) to the current list head, then set list = p so the new node becomes the head.

questions.q: When traversing a linked list with a pointer ptr initialised to the list head, what is the loop-continuation condition and how does ptr advance?
o: Continue while ptr == NULL; advance with ptr = info(ptr)
Continue while ptr != NULL; advance with ptr = next(ptr)
Continue while ptr == list; advance with ptr = list
Continue forever; ptr does not change
questions.e: Traversal processes each node while ptr != NULL, advancing with ptr = next(ptr) each iteration until the null at the end of the list is reached.

questions.q: In the routine insafter(p, x) that inserts a new node after node p, which links are set on the new node q?
o: info(q) = x; next(q) = next(p); next(p) = q
questions.e: insafter obtains a node q, stores x in info(q), sets next(q) to next(p) so q links to what followed p, and then sets next(p) = q so p links to q.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of a circular linked list?
o: The last node points back to the first node
The list can hold only numbers
questions.e: In a circular linked list the last node points to the first node instead of to null, so the chain forms a loop.

questions.q: How does a doubly linked list differ from a singly linked list?
o: Each node stores two data values
Each node contains two pointers (for example left and right) to the previous and next nodes
questions.e: In a doubly linked list each node contains two pointers (such as left and right, or previous and next), allowing traversal in both directions.

questions.q: For a node p in a doubly linked list with left and right pointers, which identity holds?
questions.e: In a correctly linked doubly linked list, following right then left (or left then right) returns to the same node: left(right(p)) = p = right(left(p)).

questions.q: Which classic problem is cited as an application of a circular linked list?
questions.e: The Josephus problem, in which names are inserted into a circular list and every nth node is repeatedly counted out and deleted until one remains, is an application of circular linked lists.

questions.q: Which is stated as an advantage of a linked list over an array?
o: It can be searched more quickly
It can grow to essentially unlimited size (bounded only by memory) and nodes are quick to insert or delete
It uses less code to implement
questions.e: Linked lists can grow to 'infinite' size limited only by memory, and inserting or deleting a node is very quick (just move a few references). Their disadvantages are being harder to implement and slow to search/access.

questions.q: Which is stated as a disadvantage of linked lists compared with arrays?
o: They have a fixed maximum size
They can be slow to search and access because each previous element must be traversed to reach a desired one
They cannot grow at run time
questions.e: A disadvantage of linked lists is that they can be very slow to search and access, because reaching a desired element requires traversing each previous element in sequence.

questions.q: In the case study representing long positive integers as a linked list, in what order are the digits stored?
o: Left to right, with the first node holding the most significant digits
Right to left, with the first node holding the least significant (rightmost) digits
Sorted from smallest to largest digit
questions.e: Long integers are stored with digits from right to left, so the first node contains the least significant (rightmost) digits and the last node contains the most significant (leftmost) digits, which matches how addition proceeds.

questions.q: When storing five digits per node of a long integer, and the sum of two five-digit groups is x, how are the low-order five digits and the carry obtained?
questions.e: With five digits per node (values up to 99999), the low-order five digits of the sum x are extracted with x % 100000, and the carry is obtained by the integer division x / 100000.

questions.q: Why are doubly linked lists used to represent long integers that may be negative as well as positive?
o: Because negative numbers need twice the memory
Because comparing absolute values requires traversing the digits from most significant to least significant, opposite to the addition direction
Because circular lists cannot store signs
Because single pointers cannot store digits
questions.e: Deciding which integer has the larger absolute value may require traversing from the most significant digit down to the least significant, the opposite direction to that used in addition, so the lists must be traversable in both directions, which requires doubly linked lists.

questions.q: In the linked stack implementation, the Push operation performs which sequence of steps?
o: Free the top node and return its value
Create a new node, save the data, link the new node to the current top, and make it the new top
Shift all nodes down by one
Search the list for an empty slot
questions.e: Linked-stack Push creates a new node for the item, saves the data in it, links the new node to the current top node, and makes the new node the new top.

questions.q: In tree terminology, what is the root of a tree?
o: The special node that has no parent
The deepest node in the tree
questions.e: The root is the special node that has no parent. Every other node has exactly one parent, and a node may have any number of children.

questions.q: What is a leaf node in a tree?
o: A node with exactly one child
questions.e: A leaf is a node with no children. Nodes that share the same parent are called siblings.

questions.q: How is the degree of a node defined in a tree?
o: The number of ancestors it has
The number of subtrees (children) of the node
The number of leaves below it
questions.e: The degree of a node is the number of subtrees (children) of that node. The degree of the whole tree is the maximum degree of any of its nodes.

questions.q: The depth of a node in a tree is defined as which of the following?
o: The length of the longest path from that node to a leaf
The length of the unique path from the root to that node
The number of children of the node
The number of siblings of the node
questions.e: The depth of a node is the length of the unique path from the root to that node; the depth of a tree equals the depth of its deepest leaf. The height of a node, by contrast, is the length of the longest path from it down to a leaf.

questions.q: A binary tree is defined as a finite set of nodes that is either empty or consists of which parts?
o: A root and a single subtree
A root plus two disjoint binary trees called the left and right subtrees
A root plus any number of subtrees
Only leaves at the same level
questions.e: A binary tree is empty or consists of a root together with two disjoint binary trees called the left subtree and the right subtree.

questions.q: In a strictly binary tree every non-leaf node has non-empty left and right subtrees. How many total nodes does a strictly binary tree with n leaves contain?
questions.e: A strictly binary tree with n leaves always contains 2n - 1 nodes in total.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of depth d?
questions.e: With all possible nodes present at every level, the total is 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(d-1) = 2^d - 1, so the maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of depth d is 2^d - 1. The minimum is d.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of nodes in a binary tree whose depth is d?
questions.e: A binary tree of depth d must have at least one node at each of its d levels, so the minimum number of nodes is d. The maximum is 2^d - 1.

questions.q: In the level-order numbering of a complete binary tree (nodes numbered 1 upward), how are the parent, left child and right child of node i found?
o: parent i-1; left i+1; right i+2
questions.e: With nodes numbered by level from top to bottom and left to right, the parent of node i is i/2 (for i>1), the left child is node 2i, and the right child is node 2i+1.

questions.q: In the array representation of a binary tree using the complete-tree numbering, an n-node binary tree needs an array whose length is in which range?
questions.e: Because a sparse (for example right-skewed) tree leaves gaps, an n-node binary tree stored by the complete-tree numbering needs an array whose length is between n+1 and 2n.

questions.q: Which traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in the order Left subtree, then Root, then Right subtree?
questions.e: Inorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the root, then the right subtree. Preorder is Root-Left-Right and Postorder is Left-Right-Root.

questions.q: Which traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in the order Root, then Left subtree, then Right subtree?
questions.e: Preorder traversal visits the root first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree. Postorder is Left-Right-Root, and Inorder is Left-Root-Right.

questions.q: In a binary expression tree, what do the leaf nodes and the internal (non-leaf) nodes contain?
o: Leaves hold operators; internal nodes hold operands
Leaves hold operands; internal nodes hold operators
questions.e: In a binary expression tree, each leaf node holds a single operand and each non-leaf node holds a single binary operator; the root holds the operator applied to the results of the left and right subtrees.

questions.q: For a binary expression tree with root '*', a left subtree that adds 4 and 2, and a right leaf 3, what value does it represent?
questions.e: The tree represents (4 + 2) * 3. Evaluating gives 6 * 3 = 18.

questions.q: For the expression tree representing ((4 + 2) * 3), what are its prefix and postfix forms?
questions.e: A preorder traversal gives the prefix form * + 4 2 3, and a postorder traversal gives the postfix form 4 2 + 3 *.

questions.q: In a binary search tree, how do the key values in the left and right subtrees of a node relate to the node's own key?
o: Left subtree keys are greater; right subtree keys are smaller
The node's key is greater than every key in its left subtree and less than every key in its right subtree
All subtree keys equal the node's key
questions.e: In a binary search tree each node holds a distinct value; the node's key is greater than every key in its left subtree and less than every key in its right subtree.

questions.q: If a binary search tree is traversed in inorder, in what order are the values produced?
questions.e: An inorder traversal (left, root, right) of a binary search tree visits the values in ascending order, which is why a BST can be used to sort numbers.

questions.q: Numbers 15, 6, 18, 3, 7, 17, 20, 2, 4, 13, 9 are inserted into a binary search tree. An inorder traversal then prints them as which sequence?
questions.e: Inorder traversal of a BST yields ascending order, so the numbers print as 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20.

questions.q: Huffman codes are used for what purpose, and roughly what space savings are attributed to them?
o: Encrypting data, with no size change
Compressing data, with typical savings of 20 to 90 percent depending on the data
questions.e: Huffman codes are a way to compress data, widely used and effective, leading to space savings of about 20 to 90 percent depending on the data; a greedy algorithm builds an optimal code from character frequencies.

questions.q: In variable-length (prefix) codes such as Huffman codes, what property must the codes satisfy?
o: Every code must have the same length
The code for one symbol may not be a prefix of the code for another
Codes must be assigned in alphabetical order
Frequent symbols must get the longest codes
questions.e: For variable-length codes to be unambiguously decodable, the code for one symbol may not be a prefix of the code for another (the prefix property).

questions.q: A max-heap is a binary tree in which the value of every node relates to its children in what way, and where is the largest element located?
o: Every node is smaller than its children; largest at a leaf
Every node is at least as large as its children; largest element is at the root
Nodes are in random order; largest in the middle
Every node equals its children; largest anywhere
questions.e: In a (max) heap, each node has a value at least as large as its children, the largest element is located at the root, and the tree is balanced with the leaves on the last level as far left as possible.

questions.q: Why are heaps well suited to implementing priority queues?
o: Because the smallest item is always at a leaf
Because the highest-priority item is always at the root and can simply be popped off
Because heaps store items in sorted arrays
questions.e: A heap keeps the highest-priority (largest) item at the root, so a priority queue can just pop it off and then re-sort the heap; heaps can also be used to sort data (heap sort).

questions.q: A graph G = (V, E) consists of which two components?
o: A set of vertices (V) and a set of edges (E)
questions.e: A graph G = (V, E) is a collection of vertices (V), which represent data, and edges (E), which connect vertices and represent relationships between pairs of vertices.

questions.q: What distinguishes a directed graph from an undirected (simple) graph?
o: A directed graph has no edges
In a directed graph edges are ordered pairs, so an edge from vi to vj is not the same as one from vj to vi
A directed graph cannot have weights
A directed graph must be complete
questions.e: In a directed graph the edges are ordered pairs (vi, vj) denoting a connection from vi to vj, so (B->D) is not the same as (D->B); in a simple (undirected) graph the two are equivalent.

questions.q: In graph terminology, how is the degree of a vertex defined?
o: The number of edges in the whole graph
The number of vertices adjacent to it
The length of the longest path from it
Its distance from the start vertex
questions.e: The degree of a vertex is the number of adjacent vertices. For directed graphs this is split into out-degree and in-degree.

questions.q: In a directed graph, what is the out-degree of a vertex?
o: The number of vertices which are adjacent to (point to) the given vertex
The number of vertices which the given vertex is adjacent to (points to)
The total number of edges in the graph
The number of self-loops on the vertex
questions.e: The out-degree of a vertex is the number of vertices which are adjacent to the given vertex (arrows going out), while the in-degree is the number of vertices which this vertex is adjacent to (arrows coming in).

questions.q: The length of a path in a graph is defined as which of the following?
o: The number of vertices on the path
The number of edges making up the path
The largest vertex label on the path
questions.e: For a path (v0, v1, ..., vk) the length is k, the number of edges. In a weighted graph the length of a path is instead the sum of the weights of its edges.

questions.q: What is a simple path, and when is it called a cycle?
o: A path with no edges; a cycle repeats every vertex
A path with no repeated vertices except possibly the first and last; it is a cycle when the first and last vertices are equal
Any path from the root; a cycle has no repeats
A path visiting all vertices; a cycle omits one
questions.e: A simple path has no repetitions other than perhaps the first and last vertices; a simple path whose first and last vertices are equal is called a cycle.

questions.q: When is a graph said to be connected?
o: When there exists a path between any two of its vertices
When it contains at least one cycle
questions.e: Two vertices are connected if a path exists between them, and a graph is connected if there exists a path between any two of its vertices.

questions.q: How many edges does a complete undirected graph on n vertices have?
questions.e: An n-vertex undirected graph is complete when it has exactly n(n-1)/2 edges. For a directed graph the maximum number of edges is n(n-1).

questions.q: What is a directed acyclic graph (DAG)?
o: A directed graph that contains at least one cycle
A directed graph which has no cycles
A graph with exactly one vertex
questions.e: A directed acyclic graph, often abbreviated DAG, is a directed graph that has no cycles.

questions.q: In an adjacency-matrix representation of a graph, what does the entry G[u][v] indicate?
o: The number of vertices in the graph
It is set to 1 (true) if edge (u,v) exists, and 0 (false) otherwise; a weight may be stored instead
The shortest path from u to v
questions.e: In an adjacency matrix, for each edge (u,v) the entry G[u][v] is set to true (1), otherwise it is false (0); if the edges have weights, those weights are stored instead of 1.

questions.q: What are the two standard ways to represent a graph in memory?
questions.e: A graph can be represented by an adjacency matrix or by an adjacency list; the adjacency list may itself be kept as a 2-dimensional array (table) or as a linked list.

questions.q: Depth-First Search of a graph explores as deeply as possible and backtracks at dead ends. Which technique is central to the DFS algorithm as described?
questions.e: DFS visits a start vertex, then recursively applies the depth-first search to each unvisited adjacent vertex, backing up when a dead-end is reached; the algorithm is naturally recursive.

questions.q: Breadth-First Search visits the graph in what manner, and which data structure does it use?
o: It goes as deep as possible using a stack
It visits nodes level by level using a queue
It visits nodes in sorted order using a heap
It visits nodes randomly using an array
questions.e: BFS visits all adjacent vertices of the start vertex, then their neighbours, and so on, visiting nodes level by level; it uses a queue to hold vertices waiting to be processed.

questions.q: A minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected undirected weighted graph has which properties?
o: It contains cycles and covers half the vertices
It is acyclic, covers all vertices with |V|-1 edges, and has minimum total edge cost
It has the maximum total edge cost
questions.e: An MST is a subgraph that is a tree (acyclic), covers all vertices V using |V|-1 edges, and has the minimum total edge cost among all spanning trees; it is not necessarily unique.

questions.q: How does Prim's algorithm build a minimum spanning tree?
o: It sorts all edges and adds them regardless of cycles
It starts from a tree containing a single vertex and repeatedly adds a least-cost edge that keeps it a tree, until it has n-1 edges
It removes the heaviest edge repeatedly
It performs a breadth-first search from every vertex
questions.e: Prim's algorithm begins with a tree T containing a single vertex, then repeatedly adds a least-cost edge (u, v) that keeps T a tree, stopping when T contains n-1 edges.

questions.q: In Kruskal's algorithm, edges are considered in increasing order of weight. What is a 'safe edge'?
o: An edge of maximum weight that completes a cycle
An edge of minimum weight that does not create a cycle
Any edge incident to the start vertex
An edge whose weight equals the number of vertices
questions.e: Kruskal's algorithm creates a forest of vertices and repeatedly merges trees by adding 'safe edges' until one tree remains; a safe edge is an edge of minimum weight that does not create a cycle.

questions.q: What problem does Dijkstra's algorithm solve?
o: Sorting the vertices of a graph
Finding the shortest path from a source vertex to every other vertex in a weighted graph
Detecting whether the graph has a cycle
questions.e: Dijkstra's algorithm solves the single-source shortest paths problem: given a source vertex, find the shortest (minimum weighted length) path to every other vertex, initialising all costs to infinity and greedily selecting the lowest-cost vertex.

questions.q: In a weighted graph, what is the difference between the 'weighted path length' and the 'unweighted path length' of a path?
o: The weighted path length is the sum of the edge costs; the unweighted path length is the number of edges
The weighted length counts vertices; the unweighted counts edges
The weighted length is always smaller
questions.e: The weighted path length is the sum of the costs (weights) of the edges on the path, whereas the unweighted path length is simply the number of edges.

questions.q: In the described adjacency-matrix code, the function join(vertex1, vertex2) performs what action?
o: Deletes the edge between the two vertices
Sets adj[vertex1][vertex2] = true to add an edge from vertex1 to vertex2
Returns whether the two vertices are adjacent
Computes the shortest path between them
questions.e: join(vertex1, vertex2) adds an edge from vertex1 to vertex2 by setting adj[vertex1][vertex2] = true; remv sets it false, and adjacent tests whether the entry is true.

questions.q: Which of these is given as a real-world application motivating shortest-path algorithms?
o: Finding the cheapest or fastest route between two cities or two computers on a network
questions.e: Shortest-path algorithms are applied to phone/Internet communications (cheapest/fastest path between two computers) and transportation (cheapest/fastest path between two cities).

questions.q: What is the difference between an internal sort and an external sort?
o: Internal sorts use recursion; external sorts do not
An internal sort holds the data in main memory, while an external sort has some data in auxiliary storage
Internal sorts are always stable; external sorts are not
Internal sorts work only on integers
questions.e: A sort is internal if the data being sorted is in main memory, and external if some of the data is held in auxiliary storage.

questions.q: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be stable?
o: It never crashes on any input
It keeps records with equal keys in the same relative order they had before the sort
It always runs in O(n) time
It sorts in place without extra memory
questions.e: A stable sort keeps records with the same key in the same relative order that they were in before the sort.

questions.q: In analysing sorting and searching algorithms, which operation is treated as the key operation whose count measures time efficiency?
questions.e: The time used is measured by counting the number of key operations; in sorting and searching the key operation is the comparison. Space is measured by the maximum memory needed.

questions.q: Using Big-O notation, the function f(n) = 8n^3 - 576n^2 + 832n - 284 is of which order?
questions.e: The rate of growth is dominated by the highest-order term, so f(n) = 8n^3 - 576n^2 + 832n - 284 is O(n^3).

questions.q: Bubble sort works by repeatedly scanning the list and doing what?
o: Selecting the smallest element and moving it to the front
Swapping out-of-order neighbouring elements until the list is in order
Dividing the list into halves and merging
questions.e: Bubble sort continually scans the input, swapping out-of-order neighbouring elements until the whole list is in order; elements thus 'bubble' up the list.

questions.q: For a file of size n, how many passes are sufficient for bubble sort, and what is its comparison complexity?
questions.e: Bubble sort needs (n-1) passes with up to (n-1) comparisons each, giving roughly n^2 - 2n + 1 comparisons, which is O(n^2).

questions.q: In quick sort, the array is partitioned around a chosen element. What is that element called and what property holds after partitioning?
o: The median; all elements become equal
The pivot; all elements less than it go to its left and all greater-or-equal go to its right
The root; the array is fully sorted
The key; the array is reversed
questions.e: Quick sort partitions the array around a pivot: all elements smaller than the pivot are moved to its left and all elements greater than or equal to it to its right; the two parts are then sorted individually.

questions.q: What is the average-case time complexity of quick sort, described as the fastest known sorting algorithm in practice?
questions.e: Assuming the pivot splits the sub-array roughly in half, quick sort performs about n*log2(n) comparisons, so it is O(n log n), and it is noted as the fastest known sorting algorithm in practice when programmed well.

questions.q: A good heuristic for choosing the quick sort pivot to avoid poor performance on nearly-sorted data is which of the following?
o: Pick three elements and use the median of the three
Pick the element at the exact end
questions.e: Picking the first element can be a bad choice, especially when the list is mostly sorted; a good heuristic is to pick three elements and take the median of the three (or pick randomly).

questions.q: Selection sort works by which basic procedure?
o: Repeatedly finding the smallest remaining element and swapping it into the next position
questions.e: Selection sort finds the smallest element and swaps it with the element at index 0, then finds the next smallest and swaps it into index 1, and so on until all elements are in place.

questions.q: What is the number of comparisons and the number of interchanges performed by selection sort on n elements?
o: n log n comparisons and log n interchanges
questions.e: Selection sort makes (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 = n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which is O(n^2), while performing only n-1 interchanges.

questions.q: Insertion sort builds the sorted result how?
o: By repeatedly selecting the minimum element
By maintaining a sorted sublist and inserting each next input element into its proper place
By swapping adjacent elements across the whole list each pass
By dividing the list and merging halves
questions.e: Insertion sort maintains a sorted list (initially just the first element) and, at each step, picks the next number from the input and inserts it into its proper place in the sorted portion.

questions.q: What is insertion sort's worst case, and what is the resulting comparison complexity?
o: When the file is already sorted; O(n)
When the file is initially sorted in reverse order; O(n^2)
When all elements are equal; O(log n)
When the file has one element; O(1)
questions.e: Insertion sort's worst case occurs when the file is initially sorted in reverse order, requiring n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which is O(n^2).

questions.q: Merge sort follows which strategy?
o: Divide the list into two roughly equal parts, sort each part, then merge them
Select the smallest element each pass
questions.e: Merge sort divides the list into two roughly equal parts, sorts the two parts individually, and then merges them; recursively, MERGE-SORT splits at q = (p+r)/2.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of merge sort, and what is its noted drawback?
o: O(n log n); it requires extra storage for a temporary array
O(n); it cannot handle large data
O(log n); it needs the data pre-sorted
questions.e: Merge sort runs in O(n log n) time, but it requires extra storage space for the temporary array, which can be prohibitive for very large data sets.

questions.q: In a max-heap used for heap sort, how are the parent, left child and right child of index i computed?
o: parent i-1; left i+1; right i+2
questions.e: For the array representation of a heap, Parent(i) returns i/2, Left(i) returns 2i, and Right(i) returns 2i+1, and the heap property is A[parent(i)] >= A[i].

questions.q: What is the overall time complexity of heap sort and how many swaps does it perform?
o: O(n log n) overall (O(n) to build plus O(log n) per rebuild) and n-1 swaps
O(log n) overall and log n swaps
questions.e: Heap sort takes O(n) to build the heap and O(log n) to rebuild it each time, giving O(n log n) overall, and it performs n-1 swaps.

questions.q: Radix sort can sort n integers in linear time under what assumption, and what is its efficiency?
o: The integers must be already sorted; O(1)
The integers come from a known range and each has d digits; efficiency is O(nd)
There must be only one integer; O(n)
The integers must all be equal; O(log n)
questions.e: If the input is a list of numbers from a known range, radix sort runs in linear time; with n integers of d digits each (digits in range 0 to k-1), its efficiency is O(nd).

questions.q: In the sorting terminology used, what is a 'key'?
o: The number of records in the file
A value associated with each record, used to determine the sorted order
The memory address of a record
The first record in the file
questions.e: A file of size n is a collection of n records, and a key k[i] is associated with each record r[i]; the file is sorted on the key when the keys are in order.

questions.q: The efficiency of an algorithm is described as a function f(n). What does n represent, and what does f(n) give?
o: n is the answer; f(n) is the input
n is the size of the input data; f(n) gives the running time or storage requirement
n is the number of swaps; f(n) is the number of comparisons
n is memory in bytes; f(n) is the number of records
questions.e: The efficiency of an algorithm is a function f(n) giving the running time or storage requirement in terms of the size n of the input data, analysed for best, worst and average cases.

questions.q: A table of records in which a key is used for retrieval is commonly called what?
questions.e: A table of records in which a key is used for retrieval is often called a search table or a dictionary; searching finds the location of a record given its key.

questions.q: An algorithm that searches for a key and, if the search is unsuccessful, adds a new record with that key, is called which of the following?
questions.e: A search algorithm accepts an argument k and tries to find a record with that key; if the search fails and it then adds a new record with k as its key, it is called a search and insertion algorithm.

questions.q: Which searching technique is appropriate when the list is NOT ordered?
questions.e: Sequential search is used when the list is not ordered; indexed sequential search and binary search both require the list to be ordered.

questions.q: For a sequential search of a table of size n, what are the best-case and worst-case numbers of comparisons?
questions.e: In sequential search the best case is 1 comparison (the record is first) and the worst case is n comparisons (the record is last or absent); a successful search averages (n+1)/2 comparisons and the method is O(n).

questions.q: The 'move-to-front' method for reordering a table for efficiency does what after a successful search?
o: Interchanges the record with the one immediately preceding it
Removes the retrieved record and places it at the start of the table
questions.e: The move-to-front method places a successfully retrieved record at the start of the table, based on the observation that a retrieved record is likely to be retrieved again. The transposition method instead swaps it with the record immediately preceding it.

questions.q: The 'transposition' method of table reordering does what to a successfully retrieved record?
o: Moves it to the very front of the table
Interchanges it with the record that immediately precedes it
Moves it to the end of the table
questions.e: The transposition method interchanges a successfully retrieved record with the record that immediately precedes it, gradually moving frequently accessed records toward the front.

questions.q: In binary search of an ordered list, how is the middle position computed and what happens after comparing the target with the middle element?
o: mid = first * last; the search always stops
mid = (first + last)/2; half of the list is eliminated from consideration
mid = last - first; the whole list is rescanned
mid = 0; the first element is returned
questions.e: Binary search computes mid = (first + last)/2 and tests the middle element; based on the comparison it eliminates half of the list, searching either the first or the second half.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of binary search on an ordered array of n elements?
questions.e: Binary search halves the search space each step, giving a maximum of about log2(n) comparisons, so it is O(log n). For example a table of 1,000,000 elements needs about 20 comparisons.

questions.q: In an indexed sequential file, what does each index entry consist of, and what must be true of the file?
o: A single key only; the file may be unordered
A (key, address) pair; the file is a sequential file sorted on the key
A count of records; the file is a hash table
A pointer to a tree; the file is a graph
questions.e: An index consists of (K, A) pairs of a search key K and an address A; an indexed sequential file is a sequential file sorted on the key that also has such an index.

questions.q: In a multi-level index, what are the first and second index levels called?
questions.e: A multi-level index is used when the index itself is too large; the first index is called the primary index and the second (an index for the index) is the secondary index.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a hash function h(key)?
o: To sort the keys into ascending order
To produce an integer that can be used as an array index telling where the data is or should be placed
To reverse the order of the keys
questions.e: A hash function h(key) produces an integer that is used as an index into an array, telling exactly where the data is or should be placed; a perfect hash gives O(1) placement and access.

questions.q: Using the division method with a table of 1000 elements, where would a student whose ID number is 1009 be stored (h(key) = key % 1000)?
questions.e: The division-remainder hash gives h(1009) = 1009 % 1000 = 9, so the record is stored at index 9.

questions.q: In the division method of hashing, h(key) = key % tableSize, what is recommended for the table size to make it work well?
o: It should be a power of two
It should be a prime number
It should equal the number of keys
It should be an odd non-prime
questions.e: For the division method the table size should be a prime number; the method is usually good when little or nothing is known about the keys.

questions.q: The simplest way to convert a character string into an integer for hashing is which of the following? (For example, 'amy' with a=97, m=109, y=121.)
o: Multiply all the ASCII values together
Add all the ASCII values of the characters together (97 + 109 + 121 = 327)
Take the ASCII value of the first character only
questions.e: The simplest method adds all the ASCII values of the characters together; for 'amy', 97 + 109 + 121 = 327.

questions.q: In the folding method of hashing, what is the difference between shift folding and boundary folding?
o: Shift folding multiplies the parts; boundary folding divides them
Shift folding just adds the parts as they are; boundary folding reverses every other part before adding
Shift folding ignores the last part; boundary folding ignores the first
questions.e: Folding splits the key into equally sized parts and recombines them, usually by addition. Shift folding adds the parts as they are; boundary folding reverses the order of every other part before adding them together.

questions.q: The mid-square hashing method computes the index in what way?
o: It takes the remainder of the key divided by the table size
It squares the key and takes the middle part of the result as the index
It extracts the first few digits of the key
It adds the ASCII values of the key
questions.e: The mid-square method squares the number and takes the middle part of the result as the index; the entire key contributes to generating the address.

questions.q: Why do hash collisions occur?
o: Because the hash function is always perfect
Because there are more possible keys than array elements, so multiple keys can hash to the same index
Because the table is always empty
Because keys are stored in sorted order
questions.e: Hashing techniques map more possible keys than there are array elements, so multiple different keys can hash to the same index, causing a collision.

questions.q: In open addressing with linear probing, what is the probe function and how does it search after a collision?
o: p(i) = i^2; it jumps to random indices
p(i) = i; if the index is used, it tries index+1, then index+2, and so on
questions.e: Linear probing uses p(i) = i: when a key's hashed index is occupied, it probes the next index (+1), then +2, and so on (wrapping around) until an open slot is found.

questions.q: What is the main problem associated with linear probing?
o: Clustering: long runs of filled indexes form, increasing the chance that further keys land in the cluster and lengthening probe times
It requires the table size to be even
questions.e: Clustering is the major problem with linear probing: it creates long groups of filled indexes, and the longer a group, the higher the probability another hash lands in it and the longer probing takes.

questions.q: Why is double hashing considered the best of the described methods for avoiding clustering?
o: It uses a second hash function so that two keys colliding under the primary function follow different probe sequences
It never uses the modulo operator
It sorts the table after each insertion
questions.e: Double hashing includes a second hash function; if the primary function collides, the secondary function makes the key follow a different route, so two keys that collide under the primary function need not follow the same probe sequence, avoiding clustering.

questions.q: In the chaining method of collision resolution, what is stored at each array element?
o: A pointer to the head of a linked list, into which all items hashing to that index are inserted
A copy of the whole array
questions.e: In chaining, every element of the array is a pointer to the head of a linked list; all items that hash to that index are inserted (at the tail) into that list, so there is no clustering.

questions.q: How does bucket addressing differ from ordinary open addressing?
o: It provides space for only one item per element
Each element has space for multiple keys (like a 2-D array), and probing is used only if all columns of a bucket are full
It stores items in a binary search tree
questions.e: Bucket addressing is like open addressing but sets aside space for more than one item per element (effectively a 2-D array); the hash gives a row and the first free column is used, with probing needed only if a bucket's columns are all full.
